chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Sayyari, from Ali ibn Asbat, who said:

I said to him, 'An issue arises for me that I must know, but there is no one in the city where I am whom I can ask for a ruling.' He said, 'Go to the jurist of the city. If that is the case, ask him about your issue. When he gives you a ruling on something, take the opposite of it, for the truth is in it.'
ai.seo_question: What should one do with a single jurist's ruling if there is no one else to consult?
ai.summary: This hadith from the chapter on Evidence (Al-Bayinat) presents the principle of 'Ikhtiyar' (preference) in the absence of multiple jurists, instructing the seeker to adopt the opposite of the single available jurist's ruling to ensure the truth is captured. Shia scholars, particularly in the Usuli tradition, interpret this as a method of 'Ihtiyat' (caution) or 'Ikhtiyar' (choice), acknowledging that while the single jurist may be correct, the opposite ruling is also likely valid, thus securing the obligation. This ruling highlights the dynamic nature of fiqh where the availability of scholarly resources directly impacts the method of deriving the correct legal status.
